task.goal: Reduce mislabeled samples in a small soil-testing lab during handoffs.
hard_constraints: Two technicians process 40 samples daily with printed labels and one shared spreadsheet; no barcode purchase.
Original samples and identifiers must remain traceable; do not relabel from memory.
Measure wrong labels, handoff time and unresolved mismatches over two weeks.
task.available_resources: Existing intake forms and last month's correction log.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Source-checked handoff with explicit acceptance
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each transfer a short, two-person verification. The sender presents the sample and its intake form; the receiver independently reads the identifier on the sample and compares it with the form and the corresponding spreadsheet row before accepting custody. This changes the handoff from an assumed transfer into an explicit check against the original record, potentially catching transpositions and transfers to the wrong row.

Add columns to the shared spreadsheet for sender, receiver, transfer time and status: accepted or mismatch pending. Only one technician edits the transfer record at a time. For a mismatch, retain the sample, existing label and intake form together in a designated hold area. Record the conflicting identifiers verbatim. Resolve using documentary evidence; preserve the original entry and append any correction, its evidence, date and technician. Never replace an identifier from memory.

Use last month's correction log to select the most error-prone handoff for the first trial. The procedure needs no new equipment, but both technicians must overlap briefly at that handoff. It assumes the intake form is a reliable reference; matching errors already present on both form and label may escape detection. The additional coordination could also outweigh the benefit if errors mainly originate elsewhere. Reversal consists of removing the acceptance requirement while retaining all traceability records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across two weeks, alternate ordinary and verified handoffs by predetermined half-days, balancing morning and afternoon periods. Keep mismatch containment and measurement identical in both conditions. Record confirmed wrong-label events per sample, elapsed handoff seconds and unresolved mismatches at each day's end, including their age. Apply the same end-of-batch source audit to both conditions and count each error once. Inspect a few transfers first to confirm that the receiver actually checks the source independently. The mechanism is challenged if checks are routinely skipped, wrong-label rates do not improve, or delay and unresolved work increase substantially. With only 40 samples daily, report counts and uncertainty rather than claiming proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fixed-position custody with a traveling manifest
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep samples in numbered positions within an existing rack, tray or clearly marked bench area, and hand over the entire group with a position manifest. Each position maps to an original sample identifier copied from the intake form and checked against the printed sample label before loading. The primary mechanism is physical separation and stable placement: technicians need fewer loose-sample transfers in which labels, forms or neighboring samples can become confused.

Record batch, position, original identifier, current custodian and exceptions in a separate spreadsheet tab. A position number is only a location reference, never a replacement sample identifier. Keep each existing sample label intact and retain the intake forms with the batch. At handoff, the receiver checks occupied positions, vacancies and manifest agreement before accepting the group. If processing requires removal, mark the position out; return the sample only after checking its original identifier. Hold unexplained discrepancies without guessing or silently moving samples to make the manifest fit.

Use the correction log to identify whether swaps between neighboring samples or lost batch membership are plausible targets. Prerequisites are sufficient existing space and a workflow that permits samples to stay in assigned positions through at least one handoff. This may offer little benefit where samples must constantly change containers or where labels are already wrong at intake. Positions can also create false confidence, so the manifest cannot substitute for checking identifiers. The procedure is reversible by retiring the location mapping after all samples are reconciled.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, allocate comparable batches by a predetermined alternating sequence to fixed-position handling or current handling. Record confirmed wrong labels, handoff duration and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages for both. Use the same source audit after handoff in both groups. Before live use, conduct a paper-only rehearsal with an intentionally incorrect manifest position; check whether the receiver detects it without relying on location alone. No live sample is deliberately mislabeled. Reject or revise the approach if position records frequently become stale, swaps persist, or maintaining the manifest takes longer than the transfer errors it prevents justify. Interpret low error counts cautiously.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One-sample labeling gate before transfer
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Prevent labels from being assigned to the wrong sample by allowing only one sample, its intake form and its matching printed label in the active labeling area at a time. Complete that sample's label application and source check before bringing the next sample into the area. Keep unused printed labels separate from completed samples. The primary mechanism is reducing opportunities for cross-assignment during preparation, before a handoff exposes the mistake.

Review last month's correction log to identify the step where labels are first applied or a labeled derivative is created. Introduce the gate there. Add spreadsheet fields for source identifier, labeling completion and next custodian. Check the printed identifier against the intake form and the sample's existing identifier before marking completion. For derivatives, record the parent identifier and retain the parent-to-derivative relationship. Never cover or discard an original identifier to make a discrepancy disappear. Isolate unexpected or duplicate labels, preserve the conflicting evidence and append documented corrections rather than overwriting history.

The receiving technician accepts only samples marked complete and checks that each physical sample has a corresponding spreadsheet entry. This requires an existing surface that can be kept clear and enough discipline to avoid overlapping labeling tasks. It assumes label cross-assignment is a meaningful source of errors; it will not reliably catch an incorrect identifier already printed consistently across all source documents. Frequent interruptions may reduce throughput. Reversal simply restores the previous preparation sequence while retaining all completed tracking and correction records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over two weeks, use a predetermined alternating schedule of ordinary preparation and one-sample preparation, with equal coverage of each technician where feasible. Keep receiving checks and end-of-batch audits identical. Record confirmed wrong-label events per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with their age; also record preparation time to expose any shifted workload. Rehearse with spare paper identifiers to inspect whether an interruption leaves an unambiguous active sample and label. The proposal is weakened if multiple samples accumulate in the active area, label errors remain unchanged, or preparation delays grow without an observable reduction in mismatches. Treat a zero-error fortnight as limited evidence, not proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep one technician responsible from intake to completion
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace routine transfers of partly processed samples with end-to-end responsibility. Assign each incoming sample to one of the two technicians in the shared spreadsheet; that technician performs its processing and closes its record. Both technicians continue working, but divide samples rather than dividing processing stages. The mechanism is reducing the number of custody changes where a sample can become associated with another sample's label or spreadsheet row.

First inspect the intake forms and last month's correction log to identify a processing route both technicians can complete. Apply ownership to that route, balancing assignments by expected workload rather than assuming every sample takes equal effort. Shared equipment can still be scheduled between technicians without transferring sample responsibility. Preserve all printed labels and original identifiers. Record owner, processing status and any unavoidable transfer in the existing spreadsheet, with one editor at a time.

For an unexpected mismatch, pause that sample, retain its label and intake documentation, and record conflicting identifiers verbatim. Resolve only from documentary evidence, appending the correction and its basis without deleting the original record. Never relabel from memory. If an owner becomes unavailable, record an explicit exception transfer rather than allowing unrecorded substitution.

This requires both technicians to be qualified for the selected route and equipment scheduling that permits individual responsibility. It may worsen queues where specialization is essential, and it cannot prevent mistakes already present at intake. Reversal restores stage-based assignments while retaining ownership and correction records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, assign comparable eligible batches by a predetermined alternating sequence to individual ownership or current stage-based handling. Give both groups the same final comparison against intake records. Record confirmed wrong-label counts and sample denominators, total handoff seconds per batch, seconds per actual handoff, and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages. Record completion time to expose displaced delays. A batch with no transfer has zero total handoff time; its per-handoff time is not applicable. Inspect the first day's records: if ownership does not reduce actual transfers, its mechanism has failed. Revise or reject it if errors persist or queues materially worsen. Low error counts will leave effectiveness uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Spreadsheet reconciliation that exposes duplicate and missing identifiers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the shared spreadsheet to flag impossible or incomplete handoff records automatically. The mechanism is a consistency check across the whole batch: assigning the same identifier to two containers should also leave another expected identifier missing. This can expose errors that remain unnoticed when technicians inspect samples individually.

Create a trial tab containing the expected identifiers from existing intake forms, preserving the original records. For each handoff, the receiving technician enters the identifier actually visible on each container into a separate observed column, formatted as text to preserve leading zeros. Use ordinary spreadsheet formulas or conditional formatting to flag unexpected identifiers, repeated identifiers and expected samples without a receipt. Do not populate observed identifiers automatically from the expected list. Process one editor at a time.

First establish whether identifiers uniquely identify containers. Where legitimate derivatives share a parent identifier, reconcile their documented container identifiers or expected multiplicities separately; do not invent replacement identities. Keep original labels intact. Hold flagged samples with their intake documentation, record conflicting values verbatim, and append evidence-backed resolutions without overwriting the original observation. Never relabel from memory.

This requires spreadsheet functions already available and time to enter observed identifiers. It assumes duplicate, omitted or unexpected identifiers explain some errors in last month's correction log. A complete swap between two valid identifiers will pass reconciliation, and typing mistakes can create false alarms. Reversal consists of disabling the trial checks while retaining the observations and correction history.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First test the formulas on copied historical or fictional rows containing a duplicate, an omission and an unexpected identifier; also include a valid two-sample swap to demonstrate the limitation. Do not alter live labels.

Across two weeks, alternate comparable batches between reconciliation and ordinary recording. Apply the same final intake-document audit to both. Record confirmed wrong-label counts and sample totals, handoff seconds including data entry, and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages. Distinguish transcription alarms from physical label errors. Inspect whether flags appear before samples advance. Frequent false alarms, ignored flags or unchanged audited errors would challenge usefulness; few errors would leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Keep spreadsheet identities fixed and record transfers separately
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent a correct physical sample from becoming associated with the wrong spreadsheet row. Review the correction log for partial sorts, pasted identifiers, duplicate rows or entries made into a neighboring row. Create a protected reference tab from the intake forms, with one record per original identifier. Keep identifiers fixed; enter custody changes in a separate append-only transfer tab using the full identifier rather than a remembered row number. Use existing spreadsheet protection and validation features if available; otherwise designate one technician to maintain the reference tab.

Before processing, reconcile the reference records with the intake forms. At transfer, find the sample by its printed identifier, record the receiving technician and stage, and flag missing or multiple matches. Preserve original labels and forms. For discrepancies, hold the affected sample, record both conflicting values and append any correction with its documentary basis. Never overwrite the reference silently or reconstruct an identifier from memory.

The mechanism is stable record identity despite spreadsheet rearrangement. It needs only the existing spreadsheet and forms, but assumes spreadsheet handling contributes to errors. It cannot detect a label and intake form that already contain the same wrong identifier. The protected reference may also become stale if legitimate intake changes are not appended promptly. Reversal means returning to the previous workbook layout while retaining the reference and transfer history.
EXPAND.experiment: The technician maintaining intake records owns a two-week trial. Alternate comparable half-days between this procedure and source-checked handoffs using the existing spreadsheet layout. Use identical physical source checks and final audits. Record confirmed wrong labels per sample, handoff seconds, unresolved mismatches and their ages daily; separately record spreadsheet maintenance time. First use fictional rows to check whether sorting or inserting a row can redirect a transfer. Stop live use if legitimate records become inaccessible or custody entries cannot be reconciled. Prefer the simpler source-check procedure if error counts do not improve and total recording work rises. Low event counts leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Make interrupted handoffs explicitly unfinished
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent interrupted transfers from being treated as completed. Use the correction log to identify handoffs where a technician was called away, work crossed a break, or a sample was left between stations. Add a transfer state and current custodian to the shared spreadsheet. Before starting a transfer, the sender records ‘pending’; custody remains with the sender until the receiver records acceptance. A pending sample stays in an existing designated area with its original label and intake form.

If either technician is interrupted before acceptance, resume from the beginning of that transfer: locate the sample, compare its identifier with the intake form and spreadsheet, and then accept or record a mismatch. Do not infer completion from a moved sample, an open spreadsheet row or recollection. Complete one transfer-state update before another technician edits it. A discrepancy remains pending in the hold area until documentary evidence supports an appended correction; preserve all original identifiers and conflicting entries.

The mechanism is a recoverable transaction boundary: interruptions leave an explicit unfinished state instead of an ambiguous transfer. Unlike an ordinary two-person check, this procedure specifies who retains custody and what happens after an incomplete check. It requires no purchase, but does require consistent state updates and enough existing space to distinguish pending work. It adds little if interruptions are rare, and an outdated status can itself mislead. Remove the pending-state requirement to reverse the trial, retaining its records.
EXPAND.experiment: The technician sending the first daily batch owns a two-week trial. Alternate comparable half-days between this procedure and ordinary source-checked acceptance. Keep source comparisons identical. Record confirmed wrong labels per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with age; also record restarts and time samples spend pending. Rehearse one interrupted transfer with paper sample stand-ins before live use. Stop if a sample has no identifiable custodian or pending work cannot be cleared within normal staffing. Reject the added state mechanism if it produces no observable labeling benefit while increasing delay or unresolved work. Report counts rather than treating a quiet fortnight as proof.

EXPAND.title: Reconcile printed label issuance before labels reach the bench
EXPAND.proposal:
Control obsolete and duplicate printed labels before they can be applied. Review the correction log for reprints, labels left from previous batches and multiple labels bearing the same identifier. For each print run, record the intended identifiers and label quantities in a separate tab of the shared spreadsheet, using intake forms as the source. Check the printed output against that list before releasing it for use. Treat this as label inventory, not as a substitute for sample identity checks.

Assign one technician responsibility for each print run. Record labels as applied, retained unused or void. Keep void and superseded labels together on a clearly marked retained sheet or in a separate existing location, away from usable labels. A reprint requires a recorded reason and disposition of the earlier copy. If an earlier label cannot be accounted for, hold the affected sample and labels until the conflict is documented. Never remove an original sample identifier to reconcile the count. Derivative labels must retain a documented parent relationship and an explicit expected quantity.

The mechanism removes ambiguous label copies from circulation. It differs from one-sample labeling because a technician can select an obsolete label even when only one sample is present. It needs existing printing, forms, spreadsheet space and a place to retain void labels. It assumes legitimate label quantities can be specified; complicated derivative workflows may make reconciliation burdensome. It cannot catch an incorrect identifier reproduced consistently from intake. Reversal retires issuance accounting while preserving its history.
EXPAND.experiment: The print-run owner runs a two-week comparison, alternating comparable batches between issuance reconciliation plus one-sample labeling and one-sample labeling alone. Keep receiving source checks identical. Record confirmed wrong labels per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with age; also measure print preparation time and labels held for reconciliation. First inspect a paper rehearsal containing an obsolete duplicate and a legitimate derivative copy. Stop if accounting cannot distinguish legitimate copies or delays necessary processing. Retain the procedure only if its labeling benefit justifies added preparation and holds; finding unused labels alone does not demonstrate fewer mislabeled samples.

EXPAND.title: Reduce custody changes through end-to-end sample ownership
EXPAND.proposal:
Remove avoidable handoffs by assigning each technician a small group of samples to carry from intake through preparation, testing and result entry wherever both technicians are qualified. Use the intake forms to assign ownership in the existing spreadsheet. Each owner checks printed labels against intake records before processing and preserves all original identifiers and parent-to-derivative links. Samples keep the same owner across routine stages instead of changing hands simply because a stage has finished.

Review the correction log and current workflow first to identify transfers that arise from task division rather than a technical requirement. Retain necessary transfers, independent checks and equipment constraints. At an unavoidable transfer, record sender, receiver and stage, and check the sample against its intake form and spreadsheet entry. If an owner becomes unavailable, make an explicit documented transfer; do not leave work informally inherited. Hold discrepancies with their original labels and forms, record conflicting values, and append evidence-based corrections.

The mechanism reduces exposure to transfer errors by reducing the number of custody changes. It differs from improving verification at every handoff. It requires both technicians to be competent in the reassigned stages and a workflow that permits individual ownership without disrupting shared equipment. It may reduce opportunities for another technician to notice an earlier mistake, so preserve the existing final independent check. If either prerequisite fails, this route is unsuitable. Reversal restores stage-based assignments after documenting custody for all unfinished samples.
EXPAND.experiment: One technician coordinates a two-week trial with alternating comparable batches assigned to end-to-end ownership or stage-based work with source-checked handoffs. Balance workload between technicians and retain the same independent final audit. Measure confirmed wrong labels per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with age. Also count transfers and measure batch completion time, since faster handoffs could conceal slower processing. Stop reassignment if required competence is missing, checks are skipped or queues threaten normal processing. Prefer stage-based work if ownership reduces transfers without improving labeling outcomes, or if delays or errors escaping independent detection increase. Sparse errors may leave the comparison inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: Improvement to P0: Source-checked acceptance with bounded handoff windows
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P0’s mechanism: the receiver independently compares each physical sample’s printed identifier with its intake form and spreadsheet record before accepting custody. Repair its main execution weakness—requiring both technicians to interrupt work whenever a sample is ready—by using short, agreed handoff windows. Between windows, the sender retains custody and keeps ready samples with their forms in an existing designated area. Record sender, receiver, acceptance time and exceptions in the shared spreadsheet; only one technician edits at a time.

Compared with P1’s fixed positions, this route directly checks identity without requiring samples to remain in stable locations. Its binding prerequisite is brief technician overlap. Its displaced costs are waiting, congestion and delayed testing; fewer interruptions alone would not demonstrate success. Review the correction log to choose one recurring handoff where identity mistakes plausibly occur. Set windows around existing processing deadlines, with an immediate checked transfer when waiting would compromise a sample. If no overlap is possible, the sender retains custody and continues only authorized work; do not treat an unattended move as acceptance. If this prevents timely processing, discontinue the window arrangement.

For discrepancies, preserve the sample, original labels, forms and conflicting spreadsheet values together on hold. Append corrections only when documentary evidence establishes the relationship, recording who corrected it and why. Matching errors already present in both label and intake form can escape this check. Reversal restores the previous transfer schedule while retaining acceptance and correction records.
EXPAND.experiment: The receiving technician owns a two-week trial at the selected handoff. Alternate comparable days between current feasible practice and scheduled, source-checked acceptance; retain existing safeguards in both. Record independently confirmed wrong labels per sample checked, total daily handoff minutes for both technicians, and unresolved mismatches at each day’s end, including their age. Also record waiting time and missed processing deadlines. Use the same end-of-day source reconciliation under both conditions to reduce detection bias. Stop scheduled windows immediately if they threaten sample integrity or deadlines; use immediate checked transfers. No reduction in wrong labels, or a reduction accompanied by unacceptable delays or growing unresolved holds, would argue against adoption. Sparse errors will limit conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Improvement to P1: Fixed-position custody with an exception gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Preserve P1’s mechanism: reduce loose-sample handling by keeping each sample in an assigned position in an existing rack, tray or marked bench area. Repair its central weakness—position mappings become unreliable when processing removes samples—by admitting only stages where removal and return can be explicitly controlled.

Before loading, compare each printed label with its intake form and record original identifier, batch and position in the shared spreadsheet. Position is a location reference, never an identity. At removal, record the identifier, destination and technician, leaving that position reserved. Before return, compare the physical label with the intake form and reserved entry. A sample with uncertain location or identity goes on hold; never move neighbors or edit the manifest merely to make counts agree. At batch handoff, the receiver checks physical identifiers against the manifest and verifies every vacancy or removal entry.

Compared with P0, this can reduce handling opportunities but requires suitable existing space and stable placement. It shifts work into loading, removal logging and reconciliation, and may occupy scarce racks. Inspect one ordinary batch before starting: if samples routinely circulate among containers, positions cannot remain reserved, or logging would delay required processing, use individual source-checked transfers instead. That alternative needs only the same forms and spreadsheet.

Keep original labels and intake records intact, and document parent relationships for derivatives. Resolve exceptions through documentary evidence and appended corrections. Retire a manifest only after every sample is accounted for; retain its history when reversing the procedure. This protects recovery but cannot detect a consistently incorrect intake identity.
EXPAND.experiment: The technician loading the batch owns a two-week trial at one suitable stage. Compare alternating, similarly sized batches using fixed positions with batches using individual source-checked transfers. Apply the same final identity reconciliation to both. Measure confirmed wrong labels per sample checked, combined technician handoff minutes and daily unresolved mismatches with age. Include loading, removal and reconciliation minutes, plus occupied rack space, to expose displaced costs. Stop a batch’s position workflow after any unexplained vacancy or unlogged move; hold affected samples and reconcile from original records before using individual transfers. If total work increases without fewer errors or unresolved mismatches, the position system has shown no net benefit. Low event counts may leave the result inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: New mechanism: Resolve ambiguous intake identities before label release
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent ambiguous source identities from entering the handoff chain. Before releasing a day’s printed labels for use, compare the intake forms for all incoming samples with existing spreadsheet records. Flag an identifier appearing on multiple distinct intake records, conflicting identifiers within one form, or a missing identifier. Distinguish legitimate derivatives or repeat submissions using documented relationships; repetition alone is not proof of an error.

The mechanism is an intake identity gate: it prevents technicians from performing apparently successful checks against an ambiguous source. Unlike P0’s acceptance checks or P1’s stable placement, it addresses whether the original identifier actually distinguishes the submitted sample before processing starts. It also differs from label inventory control, which accounts for printed copies without establishing source uniqueness.

One technician checks the forms and spreadsheet before printing or releasing labels; the other reviews flagged cases only. Existing spreadsheet duplicate highlighting can assist if available, but a sorted read-only view and manual comparison are sufficient. Preserve the original records and physical identifiers. Record each conflict verbatim, its hold location and documentary resolution. Never invent a replacement identity or infer one from sample appearance or memory. If existing records cannot resolve the conflict, keep the sample on hold pending authoritative documentary clarification. Unambiguous samples continue through current handoffs.

The binding prerequisite is access to records sufficient to distinguish legitimate repeated identifiers from collisions. The gate can shift costs into intake delays and unresolved holds, and it will not prevent later swaps between correctly identified samples. Use last month’s correction log to assess whether source ambiguity is plausible, without assuming it caused recorded corrections. Reversal removes the release gate while preserving all flags, original records and correction history.
EXPAND.experiment: The intake technician owns a two-week trial. On alternating days, perform the ambiguity review before label release or during the existing end-of-day reconciliation; retain all current safeguards and hold any ambiguity whenever discovered. Compare confirmed wrong labels per sample checked, combined handoff minutes and daily unresolved mismatches with age. Separately record intake-review minutes, samples delayed and any processing deadline threatened. A flagged duplicate counts as a prevented problem only when documents establish a real identity conflict; report flags separately from wrong labels. Stop expanding the gate if review threatens timely handling of otherwise unambiguous samples, and narrow it to explicit missing or conflicting identifiers. No confirmed source conflicts, unchanged labeling errors and extra delay would favor the simpler practice; two weeks may be insufficient to establish benefit.
